title: Tamaulipas Moves Toward Barring Dual Citizens From the 2028 Governor’s Race
excerpt: The Tamaulipas Congress has taken the first step toward requiring that anyone who runs for governor hold only Mexican nationality — a rule that would force dual Mexican-American citizens to renounce their other citizenship before registering as candidates in 2028.
content:
The Tamaulipas Congress has taken the first step toward requiring that anyone who runs for governor hold only Mexican nationality — a rule that, if it becomes law, would force dual Mexican-American citizens to renounce their other citizenship before they could register as candidates in the 2028 governor’s race.

The initiative, presented by Deputy Isidro Vargas Fernández of Morena, was admitted for legislative process on Nov. 18 with 24 votes in favor and eight against, all eight from the PAN, with no abstentions. It was then turned over to the Constitutional Points and Second Legislative Studies committees for analysis and a report.

The proposal would amend Article 78 of the Tamaulipas Constitution. Today that article requires a governor candidate to be Mexican by birth, but it does not expressly require holding a single nationality. Under the change, a candidate would have to be Mexican by birth and hold no other nationality at the moment of registering. A sitting governor would also be barred from acquiring or requesting another nationality during the term, or from invoking a foreign nationality before the authorities of another country.

The state proposal follows a federal constitutional reform — to Articles 82, 116 and 122 of Mexico’s Constitution — published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación on Oct. 7, 2026, which imposed the single-nationality requirement for the presidency, governorships and the Mexico City chief of government, with application starting in the 2028 electoral processes. States must now harmonize their constitutions with the federal rule. The Tamaulipas Congress itself approved the federal measure on Sept. 30, with 22 votes in favor and six against.

The restriction would apply starting with the 2027-2028 electoral process, when voters will choose who leads the state government for the next six years, and it would not affect whoever currently holds the governorship. The initiative’s own reasoning stresses that it does not seek to eliminate dual nationality among Tamaulipas residents, and it would not affect eligibility for other offices, such as local deputy or mayor.

That last point matters on the border. Thousands of families in Nuevo Laredo and across Tamaulipas hold dual Mexican and U.S. nationality, and dual citizens are a visible part of civic life on both sides of the Rio Grande. Under this proposal, they could still vote, still hold dual nationality, and still run for most offices — but the governor’s office would be closed to them unless they give up the other citizenship first. The committees must still issue their report before the full Congress votes, so the rule is not law yet. Webb Watch 956 will follow the committees’ work.
